strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap in functional data analysis: combining nonlinear deep architectures with interpretable, structured region selection and uncertainty quantification, which prior work (classical sparse FLR, nonlinear functional models, and DNN-for-functional-data methods) does not jointly provide.

Comprehensive theoretical development: the paper establishes a network approximation error bound for the sparse-structured DNN class (Theorem 5.4), a posterior contraction rate under the marginal prior (Theorem 5.7), and asymptotic exact recovery of the discrete support and continuous active region (Theorem 5.9). The assumptions (Holder smoothness, strong-signal proportionality, prior scaling rates) are stated explicitly and the proofs in the appendix are detailed and appear self-consistent, connecting spline localization theory with sparse-DNN posterior-consistency techniques (building on Jiang, 2007; Sun et al., 2022).

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: simulations vary coefficient shape (Simple/Medium/Complex), link nonlinearity (linear/logistic/sin/composite), and SNR, with F1/Recall/Precision as well as RMSE reported against four competitive baselines (cFuSIM, BFRS, SLoS, plus FNN/AdaFNN for prediction only); four real datasets (ECG, Tecator, Bike, IHPC) are used, two with domain-informed silver-standard regions for qualitative validation of interpretability claims (QRS window, water absorbance band).

The methodological design (B-spline projection + spike-and-slab prior specifically on first-layer column groups, mapped back to a continuous active region via spline support) is a sensible and relatively simple mechanism for turning DNN sparsity into functional-domain interpretability, and the MAP/PIP-based inference procedure with an evidence-based model-selection step for the truncation level Jn is practical.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter settings, SGD/evidence-selection algorithm pseudocode, and dataset preprocessing descriptions are provided in the appendix, and code is claimed to be included in supplementary material.
weaknesses: The core model is restricted to a functional single-index form g*(∫X(t)β(t)dt); despite the paper's framing as a general 'deep functional learning' method, the nonlinearity enters only through a scalar projection, and the true flexibility gained over existing single-index functional models (e.g., cFuSIM) is not clearly isolated or discussed — this is a meaningful modeling restriction relative to the paper's broader claims.

The 'Bayesian' inference is optimization-based (MAP plus plug-in PIPs via Laplace-approximated evidence for model selection), not full posterior sampling; while theoretically justified via posterior contraction arguments, this design choice narrows the practical uncertainty quantification claims (e.g., no credible intervals for β(t) or predictions are shown) and should be more clearly flagged as an approximation rather than exact Bayesian inference.

Region-selection precision is notably low across all methods on real data (e.g., 0.464 for ECG and 0.204 for Tecator for sBayFDNN, and even lower for baselines), indicating a systematic tendency toward overselection; this raises questions about whether the default threshold τ=1/2 and the recall-heavy definition of the 'silver-standard' regions bias the comparison in the proposed method's favor, and little discussion is given to this precision/recall tradeoff or to alternative thresholds.

The silver-standard region annotations (fixed 120ms QRS window, fixed 965–985nm water band) are heuristic domain choices rather than validated ground truth, so the region-identification metrics on real data should be interpreted cautiously; no sensitivity analysis to these window definitions is provided.

No ablation studies isolating the effect of key design choices — e.g., network depth/width, choice of τ, or sensitivity to spike-and-slab hyperparameters (λn, σ0,n, σ1,n) — despite these being central to both interpretability and the theoretical guarantees (which depend on specific hyperparameter scaling assumptions, Assumption 5.5).

The framework handles only a single functional predictor; extension to multiple functional predictors or combined functional/scalar covariates is left to future work, limiting immediate applicability to more realistic multi-modal settings.

No computational cost/runtime reporting for the evidence-based model-selection procedure (Algorithm 1), which requires training R restarts across a grid of candidate Jn values plus Laplace-approximated evidence computation (involving Hessian log-determinants) — this could be expensive and is not discussed.

strengths: Provides the first comprehensive theoretical treatment of a Bayesian deep functional model, including a non-asymptotic approximation error bound, a posterior contraction rate under Hellinger distance, and asymptotic exact recovery of the true active region on the continuous domain -- a substantial and technically involved contribution (Theorems 5.4, 5.7, 5.9) with detailed, mostly self-contained proofs in the appendix.

The methodological idea of combining locally-supported B-spline projection with a group-wise spike-and-slab prior on the first hidden layer is a natural and effective way to translate functional-domain sparsity into DNN feature-selection sparsity, cleanly bridging classical FDA region-selection and DNN sparsity literatures.

Extensive empirical validation: simulations systematically vary coefficient-function shape, link nonlinearity, and SNR, and four diverse real datasets (ECG, Tecator, Bike, IHPC) are used, with silver-standard region annotations enabling quantitative evaluation of interpretability claims, not just prediction accuracy.

sBayFDNN provides not just point selection but posterior inclusion probabilities that visibly align with the true/physiologically meaningful regions (Figures 3 and 5), giving a practically useful uncertainty-quantification capability that most competing baselines lack.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter settings, explicit SGD/evidence-based model-selection algorithm (Algorithm 1), and dataset preprocessing details are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The generative model is restricted to a functional single-index structure (linear projection onto β followed by a scalar nonlinear link g*); the DNN's flexibility is only exploited to learn g*, not a fully general nonlinear functional-to-scalar map. This narrows the scope of the 'complex nonlinear relationship' claims relative to what a generic functional DNN could represent.

Theoretical guarantees rely on a long list of regularity/rate conditions (Assumptions 5.1-5.8), including a minimum-signal/proportional strong-signal-region condition and specific hyperparameter growth rates, which are not easily checked in practice and are not connected back to the practical hyperparameter choices used in experiments.

Region-selection precision remains low for sBayFDNN and all competitors on real data (Table 1), and the associated selected regions are broader than the silver-standard intervals; the paper's interpretability claims would benefit from more explicit discussion of this limitation rather than emphasizing only recall/F1 gains.

Comparisons are made only against classical/linear sparse functional methods and simple deep functional baselines (FNN, AdaFNN); no comparison to modern generic interpretability techniques for black-box DNNs (e.g., saliency/attention-based approaches) is included, which would better substantiate the claim of being 'fundamentally beyond existing approaches.'

The inference procedure is MAP-based with a plug-in PIP rather than full posterior sampling, so the 'Bayesian' uncertainty is essentially reduced to first-layer inclusion probabilities under a Laplace-style evidence approximation; predictive uncertainty is not demonstrated or evaluated, despite the abstract's emphasis on uncertainty quantification.

No sensitivity analysis of the spike-and-slab hyperparameters (λn, σ0,n, σ1,n) or the truncation threshold τ is reported, and no runtime/scalability comparison against baselines is given, despite the added complexity of the model-selection/evidence procedure (Algorithm 1).

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in functional data analysis: combining flexible deep nonlinear function-to-scalar modeling with interpretable, uncertainty-quantified region selection, which existing FDA (linear/sparse) and DNN-for-functional-data methods do not jointly provide.

Strong and fairly complete theoretical package for a Bayesian deep functional model: non-asymptotic approximation error bounds (Thm 5.4), posterior contraction rates (Thm 5.7), and region-selection consistency including exact recovery of the continuous active region (Thm 5.9), with careful, well-stated regularity assumptions and detailed proofs in the appendix.

Extensive simulation study varying coefficient function shape (Simple/Medium/Complex), link function nonlinearity (linear/logistic/sinusoidal/composite), and SNR, showing consistently competitive or superior F1/Recall/Precision and RMSE relative to five baselines (FNN, AdaFNN, cFuSIM, BFRS, SLoS).

Diverse real-data evaluation (ECG, Tecator, Bike, IHPC) with clinically/physically meaningful silver-standard regions, and physically interpretable PIP profiles (e.g., QRS boundary emphasis, water/lipid bands in Tecator) that lend some qualitative credibility to the selection mechanism.

Thorough appendix diagnostics: sensitivity to Jn and spike-slab hyperparameters, cross-seed stability of PIPs/regions, runtime analysis, additional robustness checks under low SNR, FGAM mean-misspecification, and heavy-tailed noise, which together substantially strengthen empirical credibility and reproducibility.

Honest and specific limitations section (dependence on Jn/B-spline resolution, single functional predictor/single projection direction, identifiability under local collinearity) rather than generic hedging.
weaknesses: The core inferential quantities (PIPs, region selection) are derived from a single MAP estimate with inclusion probabilities plugged in post hoc, rather than from genuine posterior sampling; while the paper cites precedent for this practice and shows empirical stability across seeds, the theoretical guarantees (Thm 5.9) are stated for the true marginal posterior process and their translation to the MAP plug-in procedure relies on an external result (Sun et al. 2022) invoked somewhat briefly, leaving a gap between the stated theory and the actual algorithm used.

Real-data region-selection precision is low across all methods, including sBayFDNN (e.g., 0.464 on ECG, 0.204 on Tecator), and the paper's explanation that this reflects imperfect 'silver-standard' proxies rather than method failure is plausible but not independently substantiated, making the practical interpretability claims harder to fully verify.

The identifiability condition (Assumption 5.8) underlying selection consistency is somewhat opaque and explicitly acknowledged to be difficult to verify under local collinearity of the functional predictor — a common situation in real functional data (e.g., adjacent ECG samples or NIR wavelengths) — which tempers the practical strength of the selection-consistency guarantee.

The evidence-based procedure for choosing the spline resolution Jn (a key hyperparameter controlling the bias–resolution trade-off) is only shown to recover a top-3 candidate in 44% of replicates in the reported diagnostic, indicating this practical model-selection step is not highly reliable despite being central to deployment.

The method is restricted to a single functional covariate and a single (linear) projection/index direction per active region; while acknowledged as a limitation with proposed extensions, this restricts applicability relative to more general multi-functional or multi-index settings that real applications (e.g., multimodal physiological or neuroimaging data) often require.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably comprehensive within the FDA literature, do not include more recent generic deep-learning interpretability/attribution techniques (e.g., saliency, integrated gradients, attention) adapted to functional inputs, which would help contextualize the advantage of the proposed structured spike-and-slab approach relative to simpler post hoc interpretability tools.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine methodological gap: combining nonlinear deep-learning flexibility with interpretable, structured region selection for functional predictors, which existing FDA and DNN literature do not jointly solve.

Provides a comprehensive theoretical package (Theorems 5.4, 5.7, 5.9) covering approximation error bounds, posterior contraction rate, and selection consistency for a Bayesian deep functional model, which the authors credibly claim is a first in this area; proofs are detailed and appear technically careful (Appendix B), including nontrivial lemmas connecting spline-support localization to the true active region.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: simulations vary coefficient shape, link nonlinearity, and SNR, with region-recovery (F1/Recall/Precision) and predictive RMSE reported against four relevant baselines; four real datasets (ECG, Tecator, Bike, IHPC) are used, two with silver-standard region annotations enabling quantitative region-selection assessment.

Strong supplementary robustness analyses: sensitivity to spline resolution Jn, spike-and-slab hyperparameters, PIP threshold, cross-seed stability of PIPs, computational runtime scaling, and stress tests under low SNR, FGAM mean misspecification, and heavy-tailed noise, which substantiate practical reliability beyond the main results.

Honest, substantive limitations discussion (single functional predictor, single projection direction, dependence on Jn choice, and effect of covariate collinearity on identifiability of assumption 5.8), which is appropriately self-critical rather than superficial.
weaknesses: The core inferential procedure relies on MAP plug-in posterior inclusion probabilities rather than full posterior sampling; while practically justified and common in sparse Bayesian deep learning, this weakens the claimed 'uncertainty quantification' novelty, since the PIPs are approximate selection scores rather than genuine posterior draws, and the paper itself concedes this (Section 4.4).

Key theoretical assumptions are strong and partly unverifiable in practice: Assumption 5.8 (identifiability/no correlation-equivalent solutions) is explicitly acknowledged to become fragile under local collinearity of the functional predictor, which is common in real functional data (e.g., NIR spectra, ECG), somewhat limiting the practical scope of the selection-consistency guarantee.

The practical hyperparameter Jn (spline truncation) selection procedure (Laplace-type evidence criterion) is only moderately effective per the authors' own diagnostic (Table 3: only 44% top-3 accuracy, 73.5% within 15% of oracle F1), indicating meaningful sensitivity to this critical tuning choice that is not fully resolved.

Real-data region-selection precision remains low for all methods, including the proposed one (e.g., 0.464 on ECG and 0.204 on Tecator), which somewhat undercuts the practical interpretability claims even though plausible domain-specific explanations are offered.

The framework is restricted to a single functional predictor and a single projection direction per region, a substantial practical limitation for multi-modal or multi-sensor applications explicitly motivated in the introduction (ECG, neuroimaging, wearable sensing), and this extension is left entirely to future work.

Originality is largely a careful synthesis/adaptation of existing components (B-spline projection, spike-and-slab sparsity, single-index functional models, and sparse-DNN posterior theory closely following Sun et al. 2022) rather than fundamentally new machinery, and the paper's link to the corresponding code repository is missing in the provided text, leaving full reproducibility partially unconfirmed.
